# Planning rules (duration, density, frozen world, domain, tone)

## FROM 01-core.md

## §6 Duration is the single time authority

**The user-selected total duration decides everything about time.** Shot count, per-shot seconds, dialogue length, and beat count are all derived from it — never the other way round. A storyboard whose shots sum to 40 seconds when the user asked for 90 seconds is a failure, no matter how good the individual shots are.

Ask for the duration during clarify if the user didn't state one. Then derive the shot count:

| Total duration | Tight plan | Default | Detailed plan |
|----------------|-----------|---------|---------------|
| 5-10 seconds | 1-2 | 1-2 | 2 |
| 10-15 seconds | 2 | 2-3 | 3 |
| 15-30 seconds | 3-4 | 3-5 | 4-5 |
| 30-45 seconds | 4-5 | 5-7 | 6-8 |
| 45-75 seconds | 6-7 | 6-9 | 8-10 |
| 60-90 seconds | 8-9 | 8-12 | 10-13 |
| 60-180 seconds | 8-10 | 9-14 | 12-18 |

Use the **Default** column unless the user asks for fewer/denser shots (Tight) or a more granular breakdown (Detailed). The table assumes ~7 seconds per generated clip, which is what VideoExpress actually produces in practice (real clips land at 4.5-8s even when 8s was requested, because lipsync audio length overrides the slider).

**Mode fit by duration** (warn the user when the combination is off):

- ≤ 15 seconds → `single-shot` or `first-last` fits better than `storyboard`.
- `first-last` → 5-15 seconds; it is one transition, not a sequence.
- `single-shot` → 5-15 seconds.
- A vertical short (抖音 / Reels) is a 9:16 `storyboard` with a hook in the first shot; 15-45 seconds.

Every individual clip stays ≤ 10 seconds regardless of total duration — that is a platform hard cap, not a style preference.

### Edit pass — after the clips come back (acted scenes, field-tested 2026-10-24)

The shot table above sizes what is generated, not what is kept. On an acted pilot the user re-cut our 80.6 s assembly to 62.7 s in CapCut and judged it smoother; every change matches one of these rules:

- **Trim every clip to about 2.5-3.5 s.** Generate 4-5 s and trim to 2.5-3.5 s: trimming the dead air is what makes it feel fast. Our assembly used clips near full length (average 3.9 s); the user's cut averaged 3.3 s. Dialogue clips keep their line: trim to the speech window, not to a fixed length.
- **Cut a shot whose information the audience already has.** The braid-touch shot went because the mirror shot before it already showed the braid; the boy-runs-out shot went because the mother's 「下來」 already implies he leaves. A consequence the audience can infer does not need its own shot.
- **Sound effects carry place, time and memory, not every motion.** Kept: rooster, child's giggle and breathing, the hospital memory, water, the window. Cut: gasp, bare feet, shoes, braid rustle, basin set down, towel folding. One effect per shot is not a quota.
- **Order can tighten a scene.** The user moved the mother's call before the boy's close-up (the outside world interrupts before he is awake) and the shoes shot before the window-light shot (his action runs unbroken, then the ambience is a breath before the mirror reveal). Offer such reorders in the plan as 導演提案; do not impose them.

---

## §7 Per-shot density budget

Long-form output fails most often not because a shot is wrong but because each shot was asked to carry too much. Budget every shot:

- **ONE primary action beat per shot.** If describing what happens takes more than one sentence, split it into two shots. A generated clip can only sell one clear beat.
- **Spoken lines are sized to the shot's seconds** — roughly **2 spoken words per second** (a 6-second shot carries ~12 English words). For 中文 use the 字/秒 tables in §3, which are tighter still. Hard cap remains ≤ 120 characters per shot.
- **A shot that speaks does little else.** No simultaneous complex action while a line is being delivered — the model splits its attention and both degrade.
- **One simple motion per `[time-segment]` bracket.** Crowded segments produce mushy, rushed clips. Three clean beats beat two overstuffed ones.

Anti-pattern: a 6-shot / 30-second storyboard where every shot has an entrance, a prop interaction, a line of dialogue, and an exit. That is four beats per shot in a five-second clip; the render will be a blur.

## §9 Continuity ledger — what varies, what is frozen

Before writing shot 1, fix the facts of the world. Everything in the frozen column stays identical across every shot unless the user asked for the change or the plan declares an arc up front; everything in the varying column SHOULD change shot to shot, because repetition there reads as a placeholder.

| Frozen across shots (facts) | Free to vary across shots (description and craft) |
|------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Location identity, and which room / corner is which | Which corner or angle of that location a shot uses |
| Time of day | The wording of the lighting and atmosphere description |
| Weather, season | Framing within the allowed family |
| Wardrobe, hairstyle, accessories | Which one or two continuity-anchor traits get cited |
| Props present, and their scale (§8) | The action and the emotional beat |
| Character physical state (clean / dirty / injured), unless events changed it | Shot duration and beat structure |

**The most-misread rule in this whole knowledge base**: "vary the lighting descriptor between shots" means vary the **wording**, never the **fact**.

✅ Same room, same hour, different sentences — this is the intent:

- Shot 2: `warm afternoon light falling across the wooden counter`
- Shot 4: `soft daylight from the side window, gentle highlights on the glass`

❌ Same project drifting through time — this is the failure:

- Shot 2: `bright afternoon sunlight through the window`
- Shot 4: `warm evening lamplight, city lights outside`

### Multiple locations are welcome; unmotivated jumps are not

Several settings make a video richer, and adjacent spaces are the easy win — kitchen → dining table → living room, or counter → seating area → shopfront. Two conditions:

1. **Plausibly one continuous reality**: the same building or block, the same time of day, the same weather.
2. **Motivated by the action**: the actor carries the cup, walks through the doorway, sits down. A cut to a new room with no reason to be there reads as a different video.

### Time-of-day changes are a storyboard-level decision

Morning → dusk → night is a legitimate and powerful arc, but it is decided **during clarify, before shot 1**, never improvised per shot. When the user wants one:

- Name the arc up front (`前 3 shot 午後 → shot 4-5 黃昏 → shot 6 夜間`) and confirm it.
- Write each shot's time of day explicitly in its prompt — `晨間柔光` / `正午直射陽光` / `黃昏暖橘光` / `傍晚 blue hour` / `夜間月光` — not "lighting matches the previous shot".
- Keep it monotonic. Time does not run backwards inside one sequence.
- Remember the cost: a time jump also changes wardrobe plausibility, ambient sound, and who is around. Only spend it when the story gains something.

Absent such an arc, every shot in the storyboard happens within the same hour.

## §11 Continuity locks — absorbed from the official VideoExpress agent workflows (2026-09-18)

VideoExpress published two browser-agent workflows (a slow-English 3D story film, v7.1, and a kids music video). Their QA logs name failures we had no rule for: an unreferenced neighbour rendered wearing the baker's apron while the baker lost hers; two children swapping jackets mid-clip; a puppy teleporting in 6 of 13 clips; a scooter and a gate materialising; a duplicated handlebar; a bicycle riding backwards; mouths moving in shots with no line. These locks are the parts that do not conflict with our own measurements. **Status: official evidence, not yet re-tested in our own VideoExpress runs.** Three official rules that do conflict with ours (no push-in camera, a neutral-only delivery word list, every shot must travel) are held back pending an A/B.

Every lock sentence is repeated **word for word** wherever it applies; a paraphrase is weaker.

- **Closed cast.** Every human in any frame is a declared Actor with a portrait. Never render an unreferenced person (shopkeeper, passer-by, crowd, a face in a window): the consistent-character model dresses them in an Actor's wardrobe and strips it from the Actor. A role that needs a third person happens off-frame (the box is left on the doorstep, the doorbell is pressed). `[IDENTITY / CONTINUITY]` states the head count: `Exactly one person in frame` / `Exactly two people in frame`.
- **Wardrobes never overlap.** Two Actors share no garment type, silhouette or colour family: a dress with trousers, a jacket with a T-shirt, boots with sneakers, far-apart colours.
- **Props start where the frame shows them.** `[IDENTITY / CONTINUITY]` names where every prop and animal is at the first instant, in the same words as that shot's T2I (`小狗一開始躺在藍色狗床裡；蛋糕盒一開始在男孩手上。`). The `[ACTION]` must be possible from that pose in one movement. Anything the shot uses must already be in its T2I.
- **No new objects.** `[IDENTITY / CONTINUITY]` ends with, verbatim: `開場畫面裡沒有的東西都不會出現：不會冒出新的物件、玩具、車輛、門、家具、動物或人，場景全程是同一個地方。`
- **Part count** for any vehicle or key prop: `只有一台腳踏車，一個把手、一個籐籃、兩個輪子；零件不會重複、分裂、融合或變形。` Prefer props with few parts; avoid ropes, ladders and close-up wheel spokes.
- **Travel direction.** Anything that walks, rides or rolls moves 「從畫面左側往右側」 or 「從右側往左側」, fixed for the whole leg. A vehicle's T2I shows it front or rear three-quarter, already pointing that way (a flat side profile is where motion reverses); its I2V adds that the front wheel leads and it never rolls backwards. While riding both hands stay on the handlebar; a wave or grab waits until the rider has stopped.
- **Silent faces are mouth-locked.** Every visible face in a shot with no quoted line, and the listener in a speaking shot, gets in `[IDENTITY / CONTINUITY]`: `Actor 1 的嘴唇輕輕閉合成放鬆的閉口表情，全程維持不變；下巴、臉頰與下半臉保持靜止，不說話、不對嘴、不張嘴、不露齒。情緒只透過眼神、眉毛、眨眼、頭部、雙手與姿態表現。` After it, no `[ACTION]` for that face mentions a smile, laugh, lips, mouth, talking or singing (`開心大笑` → `眼睛發亮、輕輕眨眼、肩膀微微跳動`). Freeze the mouth only, never the whole face.
  - **Face not visible** (back view, only the back of the head, a blurred foreground silhouette): no lock sentence. State it in exactly these words instead: `Actor 1 的臉全程不可見。` Never a vaguer phrase such as `臉不朝向鏡頭` or `側過臉` — those still get a face drawn. A profile or a three-quarter back view with a cheek showing counts as a visible face and gets the lock.
  - **Hand over the mouth** (a shocked or fearful gesture in `[ACTION]`): that shot's lock sentence becomes, verbatim: `Actor 1 的嘴唇閉合，之後被自己的手掌蓋住；手掌下的嘴部不張開、不說話。情緒只透過眼神、眉毛、頭部、雙手與姿態表現。` The hand is the motion; do not also say the lower face stays still.
  - **Non-human face with visible fangs or teeth** (a monster, a beast): the lock sentence becomes, verbatim: `Actor 2 的嘴部維持同一個固定形狀，全程不張合；下巴保持靜止，不說話。` Never the closed-lips sentence — it erases the teeth that identify the creature.
- **Video prompt enhancer OFF.** When Advanced Mode shows `Enhance video prompt`, turn it off: it rewrites the motion prompt and pulls the camera into a face close-up.

## FROM 00-operating-manual.md

## Actor cap

### Step 1.6 — Actor cap check

If the idea implies more than 2 on-screen actors in any single shot, raise it before generating: soft cap 2 actors per clip, hard cap 4. Offer to split that beat across shots (preferred) or note that 3-4 actors risks identity drift and lipsync degradation.

## FROM 03-domains.md

## narrative-character — 敘事｜人物

- **Default dialogue mode**: dialogue
- **Assumptions**: character-driven narrative storytelling with emotional focus on a recurring central figure
- **Subject rule**: Prioritize emotional sincerity, character continuity, clothing consistency, and tonal consistency appropriate to the chosen genre (historical, contemporary, mythic, dramatic, etc.). Treat the central figure as the dramatic anchor; render with cinematic gravitas.
- **Shot bias**: Favor close-up, medium close-up, chest-up, or waist-up framing to preserve facial clarity and emotional storytelling.
- **Dialogue bias**: Dialogue, if used, should be short, emotionally direct, naturally paced, and suitable for performance.

---

## narrative-scene — 敘事｜場景

- **Default dialogue mode**: none
- **Assumptions**: scene-driven narrative storytelling focused on atmosphere, scale, spectacle, and environmental drama
- **Subject rule**: Focus on visual wonder, environment motion, and clean staging rather than heavy dialogue. Lean on atmospheric detail, spatial composition, and cinematic lighting to carry the story.
- **Shot bias**: Use medium shots and medium close shots by default. Wider shots allowed for spectacle but central subject must remain legible.
- **Dialogue bias**: Prefer no dialogue or extremely minimal spoken lines.

---

## Tier 2 composition (referenced by 00-operating-manual.md)

When emitting Tier 2 in the generated prompt, you combine:

- `subjectRule` (always)
- `shotBias` (storyboard + single-shot + first-last)
- `dialogueBias` (storyboard only; omit for single-shot and first-last)
- Language rule (use the language from the user's idea; default 繁體中文 for dialogue if user is in Chinese context)

---

## Tone axis (2026-09-19)

Orthogonal to the domain: the domain says what kind of content, the tone says which emotional register. Added because real runs kept turning plain premises into "寫實懸疑 / 驚悚 (Thriller / Suspense)" — with no tone input the model guesses, and its default guess is dark. Apply exactly one tone rule as a Tier 2 line; in full-mode storyboards pre-fill the `Genre` field with the tone's genre; in the screenwriting ruleset add it under Genre grounding. The idea's own explicit mood always wins.

| Tone | Genre pre-fill | Rule (one sentence, positive) |
|---|---|---|
| unspecified (default) | infer from the idea; neutral realistic drama when there is no signal | Tone follows the idea. When the idea does not state a mood, keep a neutral, realistic register at the scale the idea implies — a plain premise is never escalated into suspense, thriller or horror. |
| comedy 喜劇 | Comedy | Beats land on reaction shots and mistimed actions, expressions are broad and readable, and the ending lands on a laugh rather than a lesson. |
| warm 溫馨 | Heartfelt slice-of-life | Small, concrete acts of kindness carry the story, light is soft and warm, and the ending settles into a quiet sense of safety — no villain, no twist. |
| action 動作 | Action | Every shot contains one clear physical event with a visible cause and result; brisk verbs (swiftly, at a brisk pace), never slow motion; the camera stays steady while the subject moves. VideoExpress renders fast motion less reliably — say so once. |
| suspense 懸疑 | Suspense | Information is withheld and revealed on purpose, held gazes and pauses carry the drama, lighting is low-contrast with pockets of shadow, nothing is explained in dialogue that the frame can imply. |
| horror 恐怖 | Horror | Dread comes from negative space, what is just out of frame and long pauses; faces show micro-expressions of fear rather than gore; slow pace, sparse sound. The `horror-found-footage` domain implies this tone. |
| romance 浪漫 | Romance | The distance between the two people shrinks shot by shot, eye contact is the main event, light flatters skin and hair; the ending is a small mutual gesture, not a speech. |
| uplifting 勵志 | Uplifting drama | Energy arcs from low to high, effort is shown as concrete physical work, the ending shows a positive change visible in the frame, not narrated. |
| documentary 紀實 | Documentary | Neutral observation with no dramatic escalation, natural light and ambient sound, people behave as they would when the camera is incidental. Natural default for real-interview / real-report. |

## FROM 07-experimental.md

## §1 Hard-cut pair — two framings in one generation (plan side)

Status: EXPERIMENTAL · 1 test, 3 takes (2026-10-03, watercolor, 中景 → 臉部近景): 2 of 3 cut cleanly, kept face and costume, sound continuous; the cut did not land exactly on the labelled second · idea from an external community VE skill, rewritten here.

**What it is.** One VE generation holds two framings joined by a single hard cut (e.g. 中景 0-4s, then 近景 4-8s). It saves a T2I image and a generation when a beat needs a size change but no camera move.

**Precedence.** For a row that uses it, this suspends the plan rule "one framing per shot; a framing change needs a camera move". Everything else in the plan rules still applies.

**Use it only when all of these hold:**
- **The second framing is a closer view of what the first frame already shows clearly**, from the same camera side and the same screen direction. VE sees only the first frame (the T2I draws 鏡頭一 alone), so anything the second framing shows that the first frame does not show well, it invents.
- **A face close-up after the cut needs that face clearly visible before it**: 鏡頭一 at 中景 (waist up) or closer with the face lit and turned toward camera. 遠景 → 臉部特寫 is out of scope until tested.
- Same place, same Actors, same side of every boundary, no time jump. No Actor appears or leaves at the cut. No reverse angle, no new space.
- Exactly one cut, two sub-shots, each at least 3 s, total 6-10 s. The cut lands near, not on, the labelled second: never time a sound or an action to the exact cut point, and expect about one re-roll in three. At most one action step per sub-shot (the row's two-step cap still holds overall).
- Fits a REACT or REVEAL beat: 中景 of the Actor → 近景 of their reaction; 中景 of the Actor → 特寫 of a prop already lit in their hands or on the table.

**Notation (one table row per generation, so the checks keep working):**
- 秒數: the generation total (e.g. `8`).
- 景別: `中景 0-4s｜硬切｜近景 4-8s`.
- 構圖與左右位置 / 運鏡: one entry per sub-shot, separated by `｜` (e.g. 運鏡 `固定｜固定`).
- 開始狀態 is 鏡頭一's first frame; 結束狀態 is 鏡頭二's last frame. The ledger has the usual two lines; nothing about the entity changes at the cut.
- 任務 gets the suffix `（硬切實驗）`.
